cards.front: A combination of computer hardware and software designed to perform a specific function, often working as part of a larger device.
Low-level software that directly controls a device's hardware and is usually stored in memory.
A processor that generally requires separate memory and peripheral circuits to function.
A small computer on a single chip that includes a processor, memory, and peripheral interfaces.
An integrated circuit that contains several processors and interfaces all on one chip.
An integrated circuit that can be configured by a user to perform different custom hardware functions.
An integrated circuit designed for a specific function that is efficient when the function will not change.
A device that converts physical information from the environment into an electrical signal.
A component that changes an analog signal into a digital signal so a processor can read it.
A component that changes digital processor data into an analog signal.
A device that produces or controls a physical action or output based on system signals.
An operating system designed to manage task execution and hardware communication according to strict timing rules.
Small and portable embedded systems, such as smartphones or wearables.
Embedded systems connected to a network to send or receive data from other systems.
Embedded systems that perform a specialized task independently without relying on a host system.
Small-scale embedded systems that typically rely on an 8-bit microcontroller.
Software architecture where simple routines are repeatedly called in sequence to manage hardware functions.
Software architecture where specific hardware events pause main execution to trigger specific tasks.
Software architecture where running tasks voluntarily cooperate to share processor time.
The process of finding and fixing problems in embedded software or hardware systems.
A Google suite of cloud-based tools and services for building, managing, and growing mobile and web applications.
A database model that does not require traditional table-based structures or rigid schemas.
Firebase's original cloud-based NoSQL database optimized for fast data synchronization across clients, structured like a large JSON file.
A flexible, scalable NoSQL document database provided by Firebase that organizes data into key-value documents and collections.
Firebase service that checks and manages the identity of application users.
Service allowing developers to remotely change application appearance or behavior without publishing a new app version.
Cross-platform messaging service that enables sending notification messages and data messages to users.
Service providing real-time crash reporting and actionable stack traces to help debug app stability.
Firebase service providing insight into the performance characteristics and network latencies of an application.
Service allowing developers to distribute pre-release versions of apps to trusted testers for early feedback.
Analytics tool measuring user engagement, event tracking, and in-app behavior metrics.
Tool using machine learning on analytics data to group users into segments based on predicted behaviors.
Smart URLs that direct existing or potential users to specific content locations inside an app.
Feature comparing different user experience variations against each other to identify the most effective design or setting.
The online chat service built by James Tamplin and Andrew Lee from which Firebase originally evolved.
A bridge or set of defined protocols allowing two software applications to communicate with each other.
The specific Firebase category containing Realtime Database, Firestore, Authentication, Remote Config, and FCM.
The specific Firebase category containing Crashlytics, Performance Monitoring, and App Distribution.
The specific Firebase category containing Analytics, Predictions, Dynamic Links, and A/B Testing.
An advantage of Firebase that makes it accessible for beginner projects and early prototyping.
The main computational component of an embedded system that accepts inputs, processes data, and yields output.
The processor sub-unit responsible for fetching instructions from memory.
The processor sub-unit containing the ALU and circuits executing data transfer, conversion, and program control logic.
The fundamental operational sequence where a processor retrieves an instruction and executes it repeatedly in order.
A processor with a flexible instruction set architecture designed to handle a broad range of computing tasks.
Category of instructions performing basic mathematical operations like addition, subtraction, or multiplication.
Category of instructions performing comparisons and logical bit operations like AND, OR, XOR, or NOT.
Category of instructions managing program flow, including conditional jumps, loops, and return statements.
A single VLSI chip housing a CPU that typically relies on external peripherals and memory buses.
An integrated single-chip microcomputer housing a processor CPU, limited program memory, and built-in I/O capabilities.
A microprocessor specifically tailored for embedded systems, integrating peripherals on-chip to save power and space.
A specialized embedded processor engineered for high-speed mathematical operations required in processing audio, video, and signals.
A microprocessor-based system-on-a-chip designed explicitly for real-time digital streaming video or image rendering.
An integrated circuit dedicated to a specific application domain and commercialized to multiple client users.
A SoC processor built by pairing a minimal core instruction set architecture with configurable logic for custom instructions.
The hardware density standard representing full CPU integration onto a single silicon die.
Application domain typically handled by microprocessors rather than microcontrollers due to high compute demands.
Application domain ideal for microcontrollers due to integrated real-time control peripherals.
Common DSP field analyzing wave data, sensor echoes, and radio detection patterns.
Specialized processor type that can easily outperform general-purpose processors in graphics rendering tasks.
The shared physical bus carrying data, address, and control signals between CPU, memory, and peripheral modules.
Computer architecture where instructions and data share the same single memory space and unified transmission bus.
The performance limitation that occurs when shared instruction and data access limits memory bus throughput.
Computer architecture utilizing separate memory units and dedicated independent buses for instructions versus data.
Dedicated high-speed memory cache restricted exclusively to storing code instructions in a Harvard structure.
Dedicated high-speed memory cache restricted exclusively to storing operational data variables in a Harvard structure.
Processor architecture designed around a small, uniform instruction set optimized for quick execution in a pipeline.
Processor architecture featuring a diverse, complex instruction set with varying instruction lengths.
Internal elementary operations executed inside a modern processor core after decoding complex macro instructions.
The original high-level machine code instruction (such as standard x86) prior to internal CPU micro-op decoding.
The internal optimization process of merging multiple decoded macro-ops into a single executed micro-op.
Architectural feature in modern x86 chips used to break down complex macro instructions into RISC-like execution units.
Processor architecture category featuring legacy x86 instructions.
Common embedded architecture family known for simple instructions, widely utilized alongside ARM and MIPS.
Hardware technique used in processors to overlay execution steps of multiple instructions in a sequence.
High-speed memory component positioned between CPU and main memory to reduce bus delays.
Alternative name for Von Neumann architecture based on the location where it was researched.
Primary architectural reason Harvard architecture excels at digital signal processing (DSP) operations.
Internal register architecture strategy used by RISC systems to balance reduced command complexity.
Major processor architecture standard listed alongside RISC, CISC, MIPS, and PowerPC as widely used in embedded microprocessors.
A re-programmable, multifunctional, automatic machine designed to replace humans in hazardous or repetitive work.
The science and field of study focused on designing and building efficient robots.
The Czech writer who introduced the word 'robot' in his 1920 play R.U.R.
The science fiction writer who coined the word 'robotics' and created the Three Laws of Robotics.
The name of the world's first industrial robotic arm.
The fundamental robotics law stating that a robot may not harm humanity, or through inaction allow humanity to come to harm.
Robot component that acts on or directly affects the surrounding environment, such as a gripper or welding torch.
Robot component that converts energy into motion to move a robot's mechanical parts.
The processing system or 'brain' of a robot that handles input signals and directs its actions.
A self-contained, self-supporting robot that relies entirely on its own internal processing system rather than external control.
A robot guided by a human operator from a distance, typically used for dangerous or hazardous tasks.
Software-based entities or programs that exist only inside a computer system rather than as physical machines.
Mobile robots that move using legs (typically four or more) to navigate rough or rocky terrain.
Robots that perform repetitive tasks from a fixed position without traveling, such as industrial assembly line machines.
An annual international robotics competition founded in 1996 that promotes AI and robotics through challenges like robot soccer.
The international robot-soccer organization that hosts competitive leagues including HuroCup, RoboSot, and AndroSot.
A global non-profit organization that promotes STEM education through annual robotics competitions for youth.
A competitive sport where two autonomous robots attempt to locate each other and push their opponent out of a circular ring.
An educational program in the Philippines providing robotics and AI skills for students from Grade 4 to 12.
The award-winning space suit project created by the Philippine Robotics National Team to address astronaut muscle and bone loss in microgravity.
An open-source single-board microcontroller platform created to make interactive electronics projects accessible.
The pre-loaded software on a microcontroller chip that enables direct code uploads via USB without external hardware programmers.
The cross-platform software environment used to compose, compile, and upload code to an Arduino board.
An all-in-one integrated circuit chip containing a processor core, fixed RAM, ROM, and I/O peripheral pins on a single die.
A processing chip that lacks internal RAM, ROM, or I/O ports, using external buses to interface with peripheral hardware.
The specific primary 8-bit microcontroller chip used on the standard Arduino Uno board.
A custom code program written specifically to be executed on an Arduino board.
A physical input or output hardware connection header on a microcontroller circuit board.
A binary electrical state or signal that is strictly either HIGH or LOW (on/off).
A continuous or multi-level signal representation ranging across a spectrum of values (such as 0–255 for PWM).
The Arduino programming function used to set an individual pin's behavior as either an INPUT or OUTPUT.
The Arduino programming command used to send a digital HIGH or LOW voltage output to a designated pin.
The Arduino timing command that pauses program execution for a specified number of milliseconds.
The fundamental physical law defining the linear relationship between voltage, current, and resistance (V = IR).
A modular expansion board that plugs directly into the top of an Arduino to add capabilities like WiFi or cellular connectivity.
A Philippine-manufactured Arduino-compatible microcontroller board based on the ATmega168 or ATmega328 microchip.
A free web-based 3D modeling and circuit simulation software by Autodesk used to model Arduino projects virtually.
The output method on select digital pins that simulates an analog signal by modulating pulse width timing.
The recommended external DC input voltage range required to properly power an Arduino Uno board.
The operational clock frequency of the main crystal oscillator on an Arduino Uno board.
A hardware device that converts electrical, fluid, or thermal energy into physical motion to control a mechanism.
A motor actuator that uses closed-loop feedback (position sensor, motor, and controller) to achieve precise angular positioning.
An electromechanical device that uses an energized magnetic coil to actuate a plunger and control fluid or gas flow.
A circuit module containing electrically operated switches used to control high-power loads using low-power control signals.
An actuator engineered specifically to convert energy into straight-line motion along a single path.
An electric motor built without mechanical brushes, utilizing electronic commutation for higher efficiency and longevity.
Actuator mechanism that generates motion by heating specific metal alloys designed to return to their original pre-deformed shape.
A high-force actuator system that generates mechanical motion by pumping pressurized hydraulic fluid into a cylinder-piston assembly.
A hardware device that detects environmental changes or physical properties and converts them into readable electronic signals.
Distance sensor that emits sonar pulses to calculate object range via acoustic echo timings.
Light-sensitive variable resistor whose electrical resistance decreases as ambient light exposure increases.
A combined environmental sensor module using a capacitive sensor for humidity and a thermistor for temperature.
A sensor that measures proper acceleration forces to determine orientation, tilt, or dynamic motion in devices.
A sensor that tracks orientation by measuring angular velocity around an axis using a spinning mass or MEMS structure.
A directional sensor that detects the strength and orientation of magnetic fields, commonly utilized for digital compasses.
A non-contact sensor that detects presence, approach, or distance of nearby objects without physical touch.
Metal-oxide semiconductor gas sensor module engineered to specifically detect flammable gases and smoke.
A photoplethysmography sensor that uses light absorption to detect subcutaneous blood volume changes and calculate pulse rate.
An ion-selective electrode sensor that measures the acidity or alkalinity of liquid solutions by measuring potential differences.
Wireless technology using radio frequency signals to exchange data stored on passive or active tags.
